Yeah, well, we do have our homeless problem. I just want to be clear. But, you know, I think there's a few things that we're doing differently. And some of it's good. Some of it's bad. I mean, historically, we have made it clear to those who are housing vulnerable. You're not welcome here. And there's been stories of people getting driven out to other parts of the state. from our parts of Orange County. And of course, that's just sweeping the problem under the rug. But what we do right, and we do a lot of things right, we try to provide housing for people. We try to provide temporary shelter. We try to provide permanent supportive housing. We have some really innovative models here in Orange County. We have a B-Well campus that is a series of different types of shelters that have paired mental health services funding, i.e. the supportive part of it, with housing funding. And I think that is part of what I think needs to happen across California, and I know the governor's been working hard on this, but we need to understand that for some people who are housing insecure or homeless, the problem is just housing, that they just need a shelter over their head. And by the way, we ought to intervene early and aggressively there because the longer one is homeless, the data is very clear or housing insecure. The more likely one is to develop mental health issues, substance abuse issues, And so I always tell anyone who asked me, by the time you see someone on the streets in a state where they're clearly mentally ill, they have probably been homeless or housing insecure for many months, if not many years. We have allowed that situation to develop, and if we intervene early in that cycle, we can hopefully turn those people back into being productive tax paying members of society, your neighbors. But if we don't intervene, they end up in that state. So it is very cost effective for us as the government to try to get in early with housing. But dealing with those people who are on our streets, I think we have to understand that a lot of times they need more than just a roof over their heads. They need significant support. They need support with social reintegration, with job training, with substance abuse issues, with mental health issues. Some of them need to honestly be in institutions. But for those who are not at that stage, they still need a lot of help getting back into an integrated space. Otherwise, if you just give a roof over their head temporarily, they're going to be back on the streets soon. And that is something I think we've learned really, really well here in Orange County.
